script_old: Can you parody a famous song, sell it, and still not need the songwriter's permission? Sometimes. This is Campbell versus Acuff-Rose, a U.S. Supreme Court case from nineteen ninety-four. A rap group made a comedic parody of Roy Orbison's song Oh, Pretty Woman. They asked the publisher for permission. The publisher said no. They released it anyway, and it sold about a quarter of a million copies. An appeals court said the parody's commercial purpose, the fact that it was sold for profit, weighed heavily against fair use. The Supreme Court unanimously disagreed. A parody's commercial character, the Court said, is only one element to weigh. Parody has to work its way through the fair use factors and be judged case by case. It added that a parody may need the heart of the original, because that's what it takes aim at. Here's the twist people miss. The Court didn't declare the song legal. It sent the case back for more work on how much was copied, and on harm to the market. So this isn't a rule that every parody is allowed. And there's none of that music in this video. [loop] So before you turn a hit song into a parody, remember
